intro: This unit starts with the old writings themselves. You will meet scrolls from caves near the Dead Sea, clay tablets from the city of Ugarit, and old copies and translations of the Bible. Then you will meet the scholars who study them, like Mark Smith, Loren Stuckenbruck and Michael Heiser.

You will learn the Hebrew word elohim. It can mean Israel's God, and it is used for other spirit beings too. Then you will read the Bible's council scenes in Psalm 82, Psalm 89, 1 Kings 22, Job 1–2, Isaiah 6 and Daniel 7. Many scholars call this picture the divine council, God's heavenly court.

Readers do not all agree about these passages. You will learn at least two readings of Psalm 82. By the end, you will be able to tell a primary source from a secondary source, explain a passage, name who said what, and compare two readings fairly.
bigQuestion: What do the old writings say about God's heavenly council, and how do researchers read them?

title: Old Books and God's Council

chapters.title: How We Know: Old Books and Those Who Study Them
chapters.bigQuestion: How do old writings, hand-made copies and translations help researchers learn what the Bible's first readers heard?

story.title: The Verse That Stopped Her
story.kicker: A college student reads one short verse in Hebrew and has to read it again.
paragraphs: Nina sat in the college library with a thick book open in front of her. It was a Hebrew Bible. The letters ran from right to left. She had studied Hebrew for one year. Now her teacher had asked the class to read Psalm 82 on their own.

The first verse was short. Nina found the word for God. Then she found the same word again, a few words later. The first time, it meant God. The second time, it seemed to mean many beings. The verse seemed to say that God stands in a council and judges among the gods.

Nina frowned. She checked her dictionary. She checked her grammar notes. The word was elohim both times. The grammar showed that the first one was one being and the second one was many. She raised her hand and asked, "Who are the other elohim?"

Her teacher smiled. "That is a very old question," she said. "Start with the psalm itself. That is your primary source. Then read the scholars. Some compare it with old clay tablets from Syria. Some, like Michael Heiser, say this psalm surprised them too. They do not all agree."

Nina wrote two lists in her notebook. One said Old Writings. The other said Scholars. At the top of the page she wrote her question. She wanted to know what the first people who heard this psalm thought it meant.
story.think: Nina's teacher said to read the psalm itself before reading the scholars. Why might that order help?

lessons.title: Primary and Secondary Sources
lessons.mainIdea: A primary source is the old writing itself; a secondary source is what a later scholar writes about it.
reading: In 1947, shepherds found old scrolls hidden in a cave near the Dead Sea. One was a long scroll of the Book of Isaiah, made of animal skin. It was copied by hand more than 2,000 years ago. A scroll like this is a *primary source*. It is the old writing itself.

Other primary sources are clay tablets, carved stones and the books of the Bible. They come from the time being studied, or they are careful copies from long ago. They let a reader see the very words the old writers chose.

A *secondary source* is what a later person writes about an old writing. A scholar's book about Isaiah is a secondary source. It can help a lot. But good researchers always go back and check the primary source first.

words.d: the old writing itself, like a scroll, a clay tablet or a book of the Bible
what a later person, like a scholar, writes about an old writing
a long roll of animal skin or papyrus with writing on it

look.title: Sort the Sources
look.text: 1. The Great Isaiah Scroll from a cave near the Dead Sea. 2. A clay tablet from the old city of Ugarit. 3. A 2015 book by a scholar explaining the Psalms. 4. Psalm 82 in a Hebrew Bible. 5. A teacher's video about the Dead Sea Scrolls.
look.prompt: Which of these are primary sources? Which are secondary sources? Explain one of your choices.

check.q: What is a primary source?
choices: A book a scholar writes today
The old writing itself, like a scroll or tablet
check.why: A primary source is the old writing itself, such as the Great Isaiah Scroll.

check.q: Which of these is a secondary source?
choices: A modern scholar's book about Isaiah
check.why: A scholar's book about Isaiah is written later about the old text, so it is secondary.

check.q: What do good researchers do before trusting what a scholar says?
check.why: The reading says good researchers go back and check the primary source first.

lessons.title: Copies Made by Hand
lessons.mainIdea: The Bible's first writings are lost; what survive are manuscripts, hand-made copies that scholars compare.
reading: Before printing machines, every book was copied by hand. A copy written by hand is called a *manuscript*. The very first writings of the Bible are lost. What survive are manuscripts, copies of copies, made by careful *scribes*.

Some manuscripts are very old. The Great Isaiah Scroll was copied about 125 BCE. Codex Sinaiticus, a Greek Bible, was copied in the 300s CE. The Leningrad Codex, from 1008 CE, is the oldest complete Hebrew Bible that survives.

Scholars lay manuscripts side by side. Most of the time the copies agree closely. Sometimes one word is different. Then scholars ask which reading is older. Later in this course you will see a famous difference in Deuteronomy 32:8.

words.d: a copy of a text written by hand
trained writers who copied texts by hand
an old book with pages sewn together, instead of a scroll

look.title: How Old Are These Copies?
look.cite: Common scholarly dates: Great Isaiah Scroll c. 125 BCE; Codex Sinaiticus c. 350 CE; Leningrad Codex 1008 CE
look.prompt: Which copy is oldest? About how many years older is it than the Leningrad Codex?

check.q: What is a manuscript?
choices: A copy of a text written by hand
check.why: A manuscript is a hand-written copy, made before printing.

check.q: Which manuscript is the oldest complete Hebrew Bible that survives?
check.why: The Leningrad Codex, from 1008 CE, is the oldest complete Hebrew Bible.

check.q: When two copies differ, what do scholars ask?
check.why: Scholars compare manuscripts to find which reading is older.

lessons.title: Clay Tablets From Ugarit
lessons.mainIdea: Clay tablets from the old city of Ugarit are primary sources that show words and ideas Israel's neighbors knew.
reading: In 1928 a farmer in Syria hit a stone while plowing. It led to the ruins of an old city called Ugarit. Beginning in 1929, diggers found thousands of *clay tablets* there. Scribes had pressed wedge-shaped marks into wet clay, about 3,300 years ago.

Some Ugarit tablets tell stories about their gods. In them, the high god El leads a gathering of gods, called his *assembly*. The gods in it are called the sons of El. Some of the same kinds of words for a heavenly gathering also appear in the Hebrew Bible.

Scholars read these tablets beside the Bible. E. Theodore Mullen (1980) and Mark S. Smith (2001) are two who compared them closely. Many say Bible writers used words their neighbors knew. In the Bible's council scenes, Israel's God is at the head, not El or Baal.

words.d: flat pieces of clay with writing pressed into them while wet
a gathering of members who meet together, like a council
an old city on the coast of Syria whose clay tablets were found starting in 1929

look.title: Two Gatherings Side by Side
look.text: Ugarit tablets: the high god El leads an assembly of gods called the sons of El. Psalm 82 (Hebrew Bible): God stands in a council and judges among the gods.
look.prompt: What is the same in these two pictures? What is different about who is in charge?

check.q: What did diggers find at Ugarit?
check.why: Starting in 1929, diggers found thousands of clay tablets at Ugarit.

check.q: In the Ugarit tablets, who leads the assembly of the gods?
check.why: The tablets show the high god El leading an assembly called the sons of El.

check.q: Why do scholars like Mullen and Smith read Ugarit tablets beside the Bible?
choices: They were written by King David
They show words and ideas Israel's neighbors knew
They are part of the New Testament
check.why: The tablets use council words and ideas that Israel's neighbors knew.

lessons.title: Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek
lessons.mainIdea: The Bible was first written in three languages: mostly Hebrew, a little Aramaic, and Greek for the New Testament.
reading: Most of the Hebrew Bible, or Old Testament, was written in *Hebrew*. Hebrew is written from right to left. Its alphabet has 22 letters, all consonants. Marks for the vowels were added much later by scribes called the Masoretes.

A few parts are in *Aramaic*, a sister language of Hebrew. Parts of Daniel and Ezra are in Aramaic. Later, Aramaic became an everyday language in Israel. Some old pieces of the Book of Enoch, found near the Dead Sea, are in Aramaic too.

The New Testament was written in *Greek*. By then Greek was a shared language around the eastern Mediterranean Sea. So a reader of the whole Bible meets three languages. Scholars who study these texts learn all three.

words.d: the language of most of the Hebrew Bible, written from right to left
a sister language of Hebrew, used in parts of Daniel and Ezra
the language the New Testament was written in

look.title: Letters in Four Alphabets
look.cite: Standard alphabets of Hebrew, Greek, English and Ugaritic
look.prompt: Which alphabet has the most letters? How many more letters does English have than Hebrew?

check.q: In which language was the New Testament written?
check.why: The New Testament books were written in Greek.

check.q: Which books of the Hebrew Bible have parts in Aramaic?
check.why: Parts of Daniel and Ezra are written in Aramaic.

check.q: Which way is Hebrew written?
check.why: Hebrew is written from right to left.

lessons.title: Carrying Words Into English
lessons.mainIdea: A translation carries old words into a new language, and translators must choose how to say each word.
reading: A *translation* carries words from one language into another. In the 200s BCE, Jewish scholars in Alexandria, Egypt, began putting the Hebrew Bible into Greek. This Greek translation is called the *Septuagint*.

Translators must make choices. In Psalm 8:5, the Hebrew says people were made a little lower than elohim. The Septuagint chose the Greek word for angels. The King James Version of 1611 said angels too. Some newer English Bibles say God or heavenly beings instead.

Translations also carry books outside the Bible. The Book of Enoch survived whole in *Ge'ez*, an old language of Ethiopia. R. H. Charles put it into English in 1917. Comparing translations shows where a word could go more than one way.

words.d: words carried from one language into another
the old Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, begun in Egypt in the 200s BCE
an old language of Ethiopia in which the whole Book of Enoch survived

look.title: A Little Lower Than the Angels
look.text: For thou hast made him a little lower than the angels, and hast crowned him with glory and honour.
look.prompt: The Hebrew word behind angels here is elohim. Why might the translators have chosen angels?

check.q: What is the Septuagint?
choices: An old Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible
check.why: The Septuagint is the Greek translation begun in Alexandria in the 200s BCE.

check.q: In Psalm 8:5, which word does the King James Version use for elohim?
check.why: Following the Septuagint, the KJV says 'a little lower than the angels.'

check.q: In which language did the whole Book of Enoch survive?
check.why: The complete Book of Enoch survived in Ge'ez, an old language of Ethiopia.

lessons.title: One Word, Many Beings
lessons.mainIdea: The Hebrew word elohim can mean Israel's God, and it is also used for other beings of the spirit world.
reading: Psalm 82:1 is a short verse. It says God stands in a council and judges among the gods. In Hebrew, the word for God and the word for gods are the same word: *elohim*. English Bibles have to pick two different words.

Elohim appears about 2,600 times in the Hebrew Bible. Most of the time it means Israel's God, as in Genesis 1:1. But 1 Kings 11:33 uses it for the god of the *Moabites*. Psalm 82:1 uses it for the beings in God's council.
So one Hebrew word points to many beings. In English, God with a capital G names one being. In Hebrew, elohim is a wider word. Readers use the rest of the sentence to see which being is meant.

words.d: a Hebrew word used for Israel's God and also for other beings of the spirit world
a people who lived east of the Dead Sea, neighbors of ancient Israel

look.title: Two English Words for One Hebrew Word
look.text: God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods.
look.prompt: In Hebrew, God and gods are the same word, elohim. Which one means one being? Which means many?

check.q: What can the Hebrew word elohim mean?
choices: Israel's God, and also other spirit beings
check.why: Elohim is used for Israel's God and for other beings of the spirit world.

check.q: In 1 Kings 11:33, elohim is used for whom?
check.why: First Kings 11:33 uses elohim for the god of the Moabites.

check.q: In Psalm 82:1 (KJV), which two English words translate elohim?
check.why: The KJV says God stands and judges among the gods; both words are elohim in Hebrew.

lessons.title: Scholars Explain It Differently
lessons.mainIdea: Scholars explain the word elohim in different ways, and each one points to the text.
reading: Why does elohim fit so many beings? Scholars give different answers. Michael S. Heiser, in The Unseen Realm (2015), said elohim is a word about *residence*. It tells where a being lives: the spirit world. It does not tell what the being is like.

Heiser compared it to a word like Illinoisan. A baby and a farmer can both be Illinoisans. For him, Israel's God is an elohim, but no other elohim is like him. Exodus 15:11 asks this too: who among the gods is like the LORD?

Other scholars explain elohim in other ways. In Exodus 22:8, the King James Version even says judges for elohim. Mark S. Smith (2001) studied how Israel's writers spoke about God and other gods over time. Readers still discuss the word today.

words.d: the place where someone lives
the unseen world the Bible describes, where God and heavenly beings are said to live
a person who studies one subject very deeply and writes about it

look.title: One Scholar on the Word Elohim
look.text: Heiser explains that elohim is a word for any being whose home is the spirit world. The word tells where a being lives. It does not tell what the being is like or how powerful it is.
look.cite: Michael S. Heiser, The Unseen Realm (Lexham Press, 2015), paraphrased
look.prompt: How is elohim, as Heiser explains it, like the word Illinoisan? How does Exodus 22:8 in the KJV show another way to read it?

check.q: Heiser said the word elohim tells what about a being?
choices: Where its home is: the spirit world
That it is equal to God
check.why: In The Unseen Realm (2015), Heiser called elohim a word about residence.

check.q: In Exodus 22:8, how does the King James Version translate elohim?
check.why: The KJV says the master of the house is brought to the judges; the Hebrew word is elohim.

check.q: Which verse asks, who among the gods is like the LORD?
check.why: Exodus 15:11, in the song after crossing the sea, asks this question.

lessons.title: One or Many? Context Tells
lessons.mainIdea: Elohim looks plural, but the words around it show whether it means one being or many.
reading: In Hebrew, the ending -im often makes a word *plural*, meaning more than one. Elohim ends in -im. So how can it mean one God? Hebrew readers look at the words around it. When elohim goes with a verb for one person, it means one being.

Genesis 1:1 uses elohim with a verb for one person. So it means one God, who creates. But in Psalm 82:1, the second elohim is in a phrase that needs more than one. God judges in the midst of the elohim. You can only stand in the midst of many.

English has a word like this. The word sheep can mean one sheep or many sheep. You know which one from the sentence. The sheep is eating means one. The sheep are eating means many. Scholars of every view use this kind of *context* clue.

words.d: meaning more than one
the words, time, place and ideas around a text that help explain what it means

look.title: Find the Clue
look.text: Sentence A: The sheep is in the barn. Sentence B: The sheep are in the barn. Psalm 82:1 (retold): God stands in the council; he judges in the midst of the elohim.
look.prompt: Which word in Sentences A and B tells you one or many? In Psalm 82:1, which words tell you the second elohim means many?

check.q: What does the ending -im often do to a Hebrew word?
check.why: The Hebrew ending -im often marks a plural.

check.q: How do readers know elohim means one God in Genesis 1:1?
choices: It goes with a verb for one person
It is in a different book
check.why: In Genesis 1:1 elohim goes with a verb for one person, so it means one God.

check.q: Which English word works like elohim, meaning one or many?
check.why: Sheep can mean one or many; the sentence shows which, as with elohim.

lessons.title: Scholars and the Book of Enoch
lessons.mainIdea: Researchers found, translated and studied the old copies of the Book of Enoch, starting from the manuscripts themselves.
reading: Genesis 5:24 says Enoch walked with God, and then he was gone, because God took him. Much later, other writers told longer stories about Enoch. These were gathered into the Book of Enoch, also called *1 Enoch*.

In the 1950s, pieces of 1 Enoch in Aramaic turned up in caves near Qumran, by the Dead Sea. J. T. Milik published them in 1976. Loren Stuckenbruck studied another scroll from there, the Book of Giants, in 1997. These *fragments* are small, but they show the stories are very old.

George Nickelsburg and James VanderKam made a new English translation of 1 Enoch in 2004. Michael Heiser also wrote about these texts. Each *researcher* starts with the old writing, then explains what it may mean.

words.d: an old Jewish book of stories and visions about Enoch, also called the Book of Enoch
small broken pieces of an old scroll or tablet
a person who studies sources carefully to find out what is true about them

look.title: When the Studies Came Out
rows: R. H. Charles, The Book of Enoch
J. T. Milik, The Books of Enoch
L. Stuckenbruck, The Book of Giants from Qumran
G. Nickelsburg and J. VanderKam, 1 Enoch

look.prompt: How many years passed between Charles's translation and Nickelsburg and VanderKam's? Why might a new translation help after the Aramaic fragments were found?

check.q: What does Genesis 5:24 say about Enoch?
choices: He found the Dead Sea Scrolls
He walked with God, and God took him
check.why: Genesis 5:24 says Enoch walked with God and was gone, for God took him.

check.q: Who published the Aramaic pieces of 1 Enoch from Qumran in 1976?
check.why: J. T. Milik published the Aramaic fragments of Enoch from Qumran Cave 4 in 1976.

check.q: What did George Nickelsburg and James VanderKam make in 2004?
choices: A new English translation of 1 Enoch
check.why: Nickelsburg and VanderKam published 1 Enoch: A New Translation in 2004.

lessons.title: The First Readers' World
lessons.mainIdea: Researchers try to read an old text the way its first readers would have understood it.
reading: Think of a text message from today. Someone reading it 3,000 years from now might be confused. What is a phone? What does a smiley face mean? They would need to learn about our world first. Old writings are like that too.

The first readers of the Hebrew Bible lived in the *ancient Near East*. That is the name for lands like Israel, Egypt, Syria and Iraq long ago. People there had their own ideas about kings, gods, temples and the sky. Bible writers used words those readers knew.

So researchers ask what a word meant back then, not only what it means now. They read the Bible beside other old writings, like the Ugarit tablets and 1 Enoch. This helps them hear a text the way its first readers may have heard it.

words.d: the old lands of Egypt, Israel, Syria, Iraq and nearby places, long ago
the people who first heard or read a text in their own time and place

look.title: A Note From Long Ago
look.text: Imagine someone in the year 5000 finds a note that says: "Meet me by the L after school." In Chicago today, most people know the L is the city's train. A reader far in the future would not know that.
look.prompt: What would the future reader need to learn to understand the note? How is this like reading an old book like the Bible?

check.q: What is the ancient Near East?
choices: Old lands like Israel, Egypt, Syria and Iraq
check.why: The ancient Near East means the old lands of Egypt, Israel, Syria, Iraq and nearby places.

check.q: Why do researchers read the Bible beside other old writings?
choices: To learn what words meant to the first readers
check.why: Other old writings show ideas and words the first readers knew.

check.q: In the note from long ago, what would a future reader not know?
choices: That the L is Chicago's train
check.why: The L is a Chicago name a future reader would need to learn.

lessons.title: Checking a Claim Against the Text
lessons.mainIdea: A careful reader checks a big claim by finding the old text it points to and reading what it really says.
reading: Some books and videos make big claims about the Bible. One claim says that space aliens visited the ancient world. Another says giants built the pyramids. These claims often borrow old words from ancient texts.

Scholars read those same texts in their first languages. Heiser was one who wrote that the ancient-alien claims do not match what the texts say. Many other scholars agree. The claims often use words in ways the ancient writers never did.

You can check a *claim* too. First, ask where it comes from. Next, find the primary source it points to. Then read what the text says in its own context. A good reader looks at the *evidence* before deciding.

words.d: something a person says is true, which may or may not have evidence
facts or texts that help show whether a claim fits

look.title: Check the Claim
look.text: A video says: "An old text proves aliens built a city." A careful reader asks three questions. Which text? What does it actually say? What did the words mean to the people who wrote them?
look.prompt: Pick one of the three questions. Why does it help you check the claim?

check.q: What did Heiser and many other scholars say about ancient-alien claims?
choices: They come from the Book of Psalms
They do not match what the ancient texts say
check.why: Heiser and many scholars found that these claims do not fit the texts.

check.q: What is a good first step to check a claim?
choices: Believe it if it sounds exciting
Ask where the claim comes from
check.why: The reading says to begin by asking where a claim comes from.

check.q: What does evidence mean?
choices: Facts or texts that help show whether a claim fits
check.why: Evidence is the facts or texts used to test a claim.

review.q: Which of these is a primary source?
review.why: The Great Isaiah Scroll is an old hand-made copy of Isaiah, so it is a primary source.

review.q: What do we call a copy of a text written by hand?
review.why: A manuscript is a hand-written copy.

review.q: What were the Bible's three first languages?
review.why: The Hebrew Bible is mostly Hebrew with some Aramaic; the New Testament is in Greek.

review.q: Where was the Septuagint translation begun?
review.why: Jewish scholars in Alexandria began the Greek translation in the 200s BCE.

review.q: What do the Ugarit tablets show that helps scholars read Psalm 82?
choices: A council of gods led by El
review.why: The tablets describe El's assembly, which scholars compare with the council in Psalm 82.

review.q: Which scholar studied the Book of Giants scroll from Qumran in 1997?
review.why: Loren Stuckenbruck published The Book of Giants from Qumran in 1997.

review.q: Why does elohim need context to be understood?
choices: It can mean one God or many beings
review.why: Elohim can mean Israel's God or other beings; the words around it show which.

review.q: In the story, what did Nina's teacher tell her to read first?
choices: The psalm itself, her primary source
review.why: The teacher said to start with the psalm itself, then read the scholars.

chapters.title: God's Council in Heaven
chapters.bigQuestion: What do the Bible's council scenes show about how God rules, and how do readers explain them?

story.title: A Field Trip to City Hall
story.kicker: A fourth-grade class watches a city council meeting, and one student remembers a psalm.
paragraphs: Ms. Ortiz's fourth-grade class rode the bus to City Hall. They sat in rows at the back of a big room. At the front was a long curved table. The mayor sat in the middle. Council members sat on each side, with name signs in front of them.

The mayor called the meeting to order. A council member spoke about fixing a park. Another asked about the cost. A woman from the town came to the microphone and shared an idea. The mayor listened to everyone. Then the council voted, and the mayor read the result.
On the bus ride home, Sam looked out the window. "That was like a picture I read in the Psalms," he said. "In Psalm 82, God stands in a council. There are others there too, and God is in charge."

Ms. Ortiz nodded. "Many scholars call that the divine council," she said. "They compare it with old clay tablets from Syria that describe a council of gods. Other readers see Psalm 82 in another way. Let's read the psalm first, and then look at both readings."
Sam thought about the mayor. The mayor did not need the council members to be the mayor. But the mayor still worked with them. He wondered why a king, or God, would have a council at all.
story.think: Why might a leader who is in charge still choose to work with a group of helpers?

lessons.title: Psalm 82: God Judges the Gods
lessons.mainIdea: Psalm 82 shows God standing in a divine council and judging the elohim for being unfair.
reading: Psalm 82 is only eight verses long. It opens with a scene. God stands in the *divine council*. That means a gathering of heavenly beings with God at the head. In the middle of them, God judges. The Hebrew calls the members elohim, which English Bibles often translate as gods.

Then God speaks. He asks how long they will judge unfairly. He tells them to protect the poor, the weak and children with no parents. But the members have not done it. The psalm says they do not understand and they walk in darkness.

God says he called them gods and sons of the Most High. But now, he says, they will die like humans. The psalm ends with a prayer. The writer asks God to rise up and judge the earth, because all the nations belong to him.

words.d: a gathering of heavenly beings with God at the head, like a king's court
a title for Israel's God that shows he is above all others
to decide what is fair and right, and to say who has done wrong

look.title: Psalm 82 in Simple Words
look.text: God stands in the council. He judges among the gods. He says: How long will you judge unfairly? Protect the weak and the poor. I said you are gods, children of the Most High. But you will die like humans. Rise up, O God, and judge the earth. All the nations are yours.
look.cite: Psalm 82:1–8, King James Version (1611), retold in simple words
look.prompt: What does God want the members of the council to do? What have they done instead?

check.q: Where does God stand at the start of Psalm 82?
check.why: Psalm 82:1 says God stands in the council and judges among the elohim.

check.q: What does God tell the council members to do?
choices: Protect the poor and the weak
check.why: In Psalm 82:3–4 God tells them to defend the poor, the weak and children without parents.

check.q: How does Psalm 82 end?
choices: With a song about the sea
With a prayer for God to judge the earth
check.why: Psalm 82:8 asks God to rise and judge the earth, because the nations are his.

lessons.title: The Assembly of the Holy Ones
lessons.mainIdea: Psalm 89:5–7 describes an assembly of holy ones in the heavens, where no one compares to God.
reading: Psalm 89 is a long song of praise. Verses 5 to 7 describe a gathering in the heavens. The heavens praise God. The Hebrew calls the gathering the *assembly of the holy ones*. Holy ones is a name for heavenly beings who belong to God.

The psalm asks two questions. Who in the skies can compare to the LORD? Who among the sons of God is like him? The answer the psalm expects is no one. It says God is greatly respected in the council of the holy ones.

Many scholars read Psalm 82 beside this psalm. Psalm 89 clearly places the council in the heavens, not on earth. E. Theodore Mullen (1980) compared these psalms with the council of El in the Ugarit tablets. The psalm also shows God far above every member.

words.d: a phrase in Psalm 89 for the heavenly beings gathered around God
a name for heavenly beings who belong to God and serve him
a phrase the Hebrew Bible uses for heavenly beings in God's council

look.title: Who Is Like the LORD?
look.text: The heavens praise your wonders, LORD, and the holy ones praise your faithfulness. Who in the skies can compare to the LORD? Who among the heavenly beings is like him? In the council of the holy ones, God is greatly honored.
look.cite: Psalm 89:5–7, King James Version (1611), retold in simple words
look.prompt: Where does this council meet? What does the psalm say about God compared to the holy ones?

check.q: Where does Psalm 89 place the assembly of the holy ones?
check.why: Psalm 89:5–7 places the gathering in the heavens and the skies.

check.q: What answer does Psalm 89 expect to 'Who is like the LORD?'
check.why: The psalm's questions expect the answer that no one compares to God.

check.q: Why do many scholars read Psalm 89 beside Psalm 82?
choices: It shows there is no council
It places the council in the heavens
check.why: Psalm 89:5–7 places the assembly of the holy ones in the heavens, a clue for reading Psalm 82.

lessons.title: Like a King's Court
lessons.mainIdea: Daniel 7 and other passages picture God as a king with a court; Heiser said God shares his work with the council, not because he needs help.
reading: In the ancient world, a king sat on a throne. Around him stood his *court*, officials and messengers who carried out his plans. Daniel 7:9–10 pictures God this way. A *throne* is set. Thousands serve him, and the court sits to judge.

Many scholars say the Bible borrows this picture of a royal court to show God's rule. Michael Heiser, in The Unseen Realm (2015), asked why God would have a council at all. He said God does not need anyone. But God chooses to include others in his work.

Heiser also saw a link to people. He wrote that God wanted a family on earth too, made of humans, to share his work. Other readers see the court as a picture of God's greatness more than a team. Later units look closely at these ideas.

words.d: the officials and helpers who stand around a king and carry out his plans
a special chair where a king sits to rule

look.title: A Court in Heaven
look.text: A fiery stream issued and came forth from before him: thousand thousands ministered unto him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him: the judgment was set, and the books were opened.
look.prompt: What words in this verse make it sound like a king's court? What is the court about to do?

check.q: According to Heiser, why does God have a council?
choices: Because he chooses to share his work
Because a king in Ugarit told him to
check.why: Heiser said God does not need help but chooses to include others in his work.

check.q: What is a king's court?
choices: The officials and helpers around a king
check.why: A court is the group of officials and messengers who serve a king.

check.q: In Daniel 7:10, what happens when the court sits?
choices: The judgment is set and the books are opened
check.why: Daniel 7:10 says the judgment was set, and the books were opened.

lessons.title: Micaiah Sees the Throne
lessons.mainIdea: In 1 Kings 22, the prophet Micaiah describes God on his throne asking the host of heaven for a plan.
reading: First Kings 22 tells about King Ahab of Israel. He wanted to go to war at a town called Ramoth-gilead. About 400 of his prophets told him he would win. But another king asked for one more prophet. So they called a *prophet* named Micaiah.

Micaiah told what he had seen. He saw the LORD sitting on his throne. All the *host of heaven* stood on his right and on his left. The LORD asked who would lead Ahab to go to battle. One said one thing, and another said something else. Then a spirit came forward with a plan, and the LORD sent it.

Many scholars point to this scene as a clear picture of the council at work. God asks, the members talk, and God decides. The members speak, but God has the last word. Micaiah's message was a warning. The story says Ahab did not listen, and he did not come home from the battle.

words.d: a person who brings a message said to come from God
a Bible phrase for the many heavenly beings around God's throne

look.title: Who Spoke to King Ahab?
rows: Prophets who said Ahab would win
look.prompt: Micaiah was one voice against about 400. Why might it be hard to be the only one who says something different?

check.q: In Micaiah's vision, who stood around the LORD's throne?
check.why: First Kings 22:19 says all the host of heaven stood on the right and left.

check.q: What did the LORD ask the host of heaven?
choices: Who would lead Ahab to go to battle
check.why: In 1 Kings 22:20 the LORD asks who will lead Ahab to go up to battle.

check.q: What does Micaiah's vision show about the council?
choices: The members talk, and God decides
Micaiah was a member of Ahab's court
God needs the council's vote to act
check.why: In 1 Kings 22:20–22 the members offer ideas, and the LORD makes the final choice.

lessons.title: The Sons of God in Job
lessons.mainIdea: The Book of Job opens with the sons of God coming before the LORD, including one called the satan.
reading: The Book of Job begins on earth with a good man named Job. Then the scene moves to heaven. Job 1:6 says the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD. That means they came to stand before him, like officials reporting to a king.

One member came too. The Hebrew calls him *the satan*. The word satan means adversary, or one who challenges. It has the word the in front, so it works like a title. He questions whether Job is good only because life has gone well for him.

Readers explain the satan in Job in more than one way. Many scholars read him as a member of the council acting as a challenger. Much Jewish tradition sees him as an angel who serves God as an accuser. Many Christians read him as the devil. Job 38:7 shows another scene: the sons of God shouting for joy when the world was made.

words.d: a Hebrew title in Job meaning the adversary, a member who challenges before God
someone who takes the other side or challenges you

look.title: The Sons of God Shout for Joy
look.text: God asks Job where he was when the earth was made. When its cornerstone was laid, the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy.
look.cite: Job 38:4–7, King James Version (1611), retold in simple words
look.prompt: What were the sons of God doing when the world was made? How does that feel different from Job 1?

check.q: What does Job 1:6 say the sons of God did?
choices: Came to present themselves before the LORD
check.why: Job 1:6 says the sons of God came to stand before the LORD.

check.q: What does the Hebrew word satan mean?
check.why: Satan means adversary; in Job it has 'the' in front, like a title.

check.q: In Job 38:7, what did the sons of God do when the world was made?
check.why: Job 38:7 says the sons of God shouted for joy.

lessons.title: Isaiah and the Seraphim
lessons.mainIdea: In Isaiah 6, Isaiah sees God's throne with seraphim and hears God ask, 'Who will go for us?'
reading: Isaiah 6 begins in the year King Uzziah died, around 740 BCE. Isaiah sees the Lord on a high throne. The edge of his robe fills the temple. Above him are *seraphim*. The name likely comes from a Hebrew word for burning, so it may mean burning ones.

Each seraph has six wings. With two it covers its face. With two it covers its feet. With two it flies. They call to one another: holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts. The whole earth is full of his glory.

Then God asks, "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" Some scholars, like Heiser, read the word us as God speaking to his council. Many Christians see a hint of the Trinity. Others say it is a royal way of speaking. Isaiah answers, "Here am I; send me."

words.d: heavenly beings with six wings in Isaiah 6; the name may mean burning ones
set apart and completely pure; in Isaiah 6 the seraphim call God holy three times

look.title: A Seraph's Six Wings
look.prompt: How many wings in all? Why might the seraphim cover their faces near God's throne?

check.q: How many wings does each seraph have in Isaiah 6?
check.why: Isaiah 6:2 says each seraph has six wings.

check.q: What do the seraphim call out?
choices: Rise up and judge the earth
Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts
check.why: In Isaiah 6:3 the seraphim call God holy three times.

check.q: Some scholars read the us in Isaiah 6:8 as what?
check.why: Some scholars, Heiser among them, read the us as God addressing the divine council; others see the Trinity or a royal way of speaking.

lessons.title: Heavenly Beings
lessons.mainIdea: Many scholars read the gods in Psalm 82 as heavenly beings, and they give reasons from the text.
reading: Who are the elohim that God judges in Psalm 82? Many scholars say they are heavenly beings, members of God's council. Mullen (1980), Mark S. Smith (2001) and Heiser all read the psalm this way. They give reasons from the text. A reason from the text is called *evidence*.

First, verse 7 says they will die like humans. Why tell humans they will die like humans? The line makes more sense, these readers say, if the listeners are not human. Second, Psalm 89 places the council in the heavens.

Third, verse 8 says God will judge all the *nations*. Judges in Israel did not rule over every nation. Heiser linked this verse to Deuteronomy 32:8, where God divides the nations. For him, heavenly beings had been given the nations and ruled them badly.

words.d: facts or words in a text that support an answer
the peoples and countries of the world

look.title: Weighing a Clue
look.text: Psalm 82:6–7, retold: I said you are gods, children of the Most High. But you will die like humans. Some scholars ask: if these listeners were already human, why would God say they will die like humans?
look.prompt: Explain this clue in your own words. Does the line make you think of humans or heavenly beings? Why?

check.q: Who do many scholars say the elohim in Psalm 82 are?
check.why: Scholars such as Mullen and Smith read them as heavenly members of the divine council.

check.q: Which verse says the elohim will die like humans?
check.why: Psalm 82:7 says they will die like humans.

check.q: Why do these readers point to Psalm 82:8 and the nations?
choices: Judges in Israel did not rule over every nation
It names the judges of Israel
It proves there is no council
check.why: Verse 8 speaks of all the nations, which Israel's human judges did not rule.

lessons.title: Human Judges
lessons.mainIdea: Other Jewish and Christian readers have said the gods in Psalm 82 are human judges or rulers.
reading: The heavenly reading is not the only one. Over many centuries, some Jewish and Christian readers have said the elohim in Psalm 82 are human *judges* or rulers. The reformer John Calvin, in the 1500s, read the psalm this way. Some old Jewish readings do too.

These readers have reasons as well. The psalm is about being fair in court. It talks about protecting the poor and the weak. That was the job of human judges in Israel. Rulers and judges acted for God, so these readers think the psalm could call them gods as an honor.

Readers of this view say verse 7 is a warning. You have an honored title, but you are still humans, and you will die. Both readings look closely at the same eight verses. They come to different answers about who is being judged.

words.d: people who decide cases and say what is fair
a leader in the 1500s who worked to change the church in Europe

look.title: Two Readings Side by Side
look.text: Reading A (many scholars): The gods are heavenly beings in God's council who ruled the nations unfairly. Reading B (some Jewish and Christian readers, like Calvin): The gods are human judges who were honored with a high title but ruled unfairly.
look.prompt: What do both readings agree on? Where do they differ? Name one clue each reading uses.

check.q: Which reformer read Psalm 82 as being about human rulers?
check.why: John Calvin, in the 1500s, read the gods of Psalm 82 as human rulers and judges.

check.q: Why do some readers think Psalm 82 is about human judges?
choices: It takes place in Job's house
It talks about being fair in court and protecting the poor
check.why: The psalm's focus on fair judging and helping the poor matches the work of human judges.

check.q: How do human-judge readers explain 'you will die like humans'?
choices: As proof the judges were angels
As a mistake in the text
As a line about the sea
As a warning that honored rulers are still humans who die
check.why: They read verse 7 as reminding rulers that they are still mortal humans.

lessons.title: Jesus Quotes Psalm 82
lessons.mainIdea: In John 10:34, Jesus quotes Psalm 82:6, and readers on both sides use this passage.
reading: Psalm 82 also appears in the New Testament. In John 10, some people are upset with Jesus. They say he is claiming to be God. In John 10:34, Jesus answers with Psalm 82:6: "Is it not written in your law, I said, Ye are gods?" That is the King James Version.

In the next verse, Jesus says Scripture called them gods, unto whom the word of God came. Readers who hold the human-judge view point to this line. They say it shows the gods were humans who received God's word.

Readers who see heavenly beings in Psalm 82 explain Jesus' words in a different way. The *Gospel* of John does not stop to explain the psalm. So readers keep studying this passage. It is one reason Psalm 82 is discussed so much.

words.d: one of the four New Testament books about Jesus: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John
to repeat someone's exact words

look.title: Jesus Answers
look.text: Is it not written in your law, I said, Ye are gods?
look.prompt: Which psalm is Jesus quoting here? Why might two groups of readers both use this verse?

check.q: Which verse of Psalm 82 does Jesus quote in John 10:34?
check.why: Jesus quotes Psalm 82:6, 'I said, Ye are gods.'

check.q: Why do human-judge readers point to John 10:35?
choices: It says the gods were stars
It says the gods were those to whom the word of God came
check.why: They read 'unto whom the word of God came' as pointing to humans.

check.q: What is a Gospel?
choices: One of four New Testament books about Jesus
check.why: The Gospels are Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, books about Jesus.

lessons.title: Comparing Readings Fairly
lessons.mainIdea: A fair reader can explain each reading, with its clues, without making fun of either one.
reading: You have now seen two ways to read Psalm 82. How can you compare them fairly? Start by saying each reading in words its own readers would agree with. Then name the clues each one uses. That is called stating a view *fairly*.

Next, check each clue in the primary source itself. Find verse 7. Find verse 8. Read Psalm 89:5–7 and John 10:34–35. Ask what each passage says before you ask what it means. Every careful researcher starts there.

Last, remember that readers have discussed these verses for a very long time. Thoughtful people have reached different answers. You can explain what one scholar argued and what others argued. You do not need to make fun of anyone to do it well.

words.d: in a way that is honest and gives each side a full hearing
a reader's explanation of what a text means

look.title: A Fair Report
look.text: Student A writes: Many scholars read the gods in Psalm 82 as heavenly beings, because of verses 7 and 8 and Psalm 89. Student B writes: That reading is right and anyone else is silly. Student C writes: Some readers, like Calvin, see human judges because the psalm is about fair courts.
look.prompt: Which reports are fair? What would you change in the one that is not?

check.q: What is the first step in comparing two readings fairly?
choices: Say each reading in words its own readers would agree with
check.why: A fair comparison begins by stating each view the way its own readers would.

check.q: What should you ask before asking what a passage means?
check.why: The reading says to ask what each passage says first.

check.q: What is an interpretation?
choices: A reader's explanation of what a text means
check.why: An interpretation is one reader's explanation of a text's meaning.

choices: A gathering of heavenly beings with God at the head
review.why: The divine council is God's heavenly court, as in Psalm 82:1.

review.q: Which passage shows Micaiah's vision of the host of heaven?
review.why: Micaiah describes the LORD on his throne with the host of heaven in 1 Kings 22:19–23.

review.q: In which book do the sons of God come before the LORD, along with the satan?
review.why: Job 1–2 shows the sons of God and the satan before the LORD.

review.q: Which heavenly beings have six wings in Isaiah 6?
review.why: Isaiah 6:2 describes seraphim with six wings each.

review.q: Which psalm places the assembly of the holy ones in the heavens?
review.why: Psalm 89:5–7 speaks of the heavens and the assembly of the holy ones.

review.q: Which book pictures a heavenly court where thousands serve God and the books are opened?
review.why: Daniel 7:9–10 pictures God's throne, a great court and the books opened.

review.q: How do the heavenly-being reading and the human-judge reading of Psalm 82 differ?
choices: One sees heavenly beings; the other sees human rulers
One sees human rulers; the other sees seraphim
Both say the psalm is about Job
review.why: Many scholars read heavenly beings; others, like Calvin, read human judges.

review.q: In the story, what reminded Sam of Psalm 82?
choices: A city council meeting led by the mayor
A clay tablet at a museum
review.why: Sam saw the mayor leading the council and thought of God standing in the divine council.
